label: Engineering Implementation
description: Land it, in an order that keeps the tree green at every step, with the unit tests that defend phase-4 invariants written here beside the code they check (feature.md §5). Four separate rules, each about one child — the confirm skip on explore, the abort on confirm, the implementation/design split on classify, the refine loop on critique — so each is eligible only in the round its own child ended.

from your own critique: they are looking at what your output made possible, not at
whether it is well made. Fix what they name, or say plainly why they are wrong.

or what another state may have edited since; re-reading the rest is the largest single

**These are paths, not contents.** Open each one with `read_file` before you start. Read the
file as it is now — an earlier state in this phase may have edited it since the run began.


## How to work

Work **change by change**, in the plan's order. After each one the tree builds
and the existing suite passes — a change that leaves it red is not a change, it
is half of one.

Before you start, be able to answer these about the plan you were handed:

1. What is the smallest thing that can land and be **useful — or at least safe —
   on its own**?
2. What order keeps the tree working? What hides behind a flag until the rest
   arrives?
3. What depends on what, and what could go in parallel?
4. What is **deleted**? Does the old path go in this change, or a named
   follow-up?
5. What rolls back independently, and what is a one-way door?
6. What does "done" mean for each change — **the observable, not the intent**?
7. Which docs does this make wrong the moment it lands?

If the plan does not survive those questions, say so in the change list rather
than quietly building something else.

## Do not write the tests

A separate agent instance writes the unit tests, from the invariants rather than
from your diff. That separation is deliberate: an agent that writes a test right
after writing the code tests what it built, not what was specified. Leave the
seams reachable and leave the tests alone.

## What to produce

`changes` — one row per change, in the order they landed: what it does, what it
depends on, its `done_when` **observable**, and its `doc_updates` (which docs it
makes wrong).

`standards_amendment` — only when `standards.md` itself is wrong. A departure
from it is an exception (with the reason, recorded) or an amendment. Never
silence: phase 8's standards row finds silent departures.

`responses` — one entry per finding you were handed above, in the same order, and
nothing at all on a first pass:

```
{ "severity": "significant",
  "claim": "<the finding, as it was put to you>",
  "target_id": "<the id it is about>",
  "disposition": "fixed" | "rejected" | "blocked",
  "note": "what changed | why the finding is wrong | what you would need" }
```

`note` is required for `rejected` and `blocked`. This is the only memory the loop has of
its own passes: the critique reads it to tell an answered finding from a restated one.

Saying you are stuck is a real answer, not a failure. If a finding asks for something
this phase cannot produce — a measurement nobody has taken, a decision only a person can
make, a fact that is not in the repo — mark it `blocked` and name what you would need.
Three passes defending a gap costs more than asking once.

Land this, one change at a time, in an order that keeps the tree green at every
step.

inputs.returned_findings.description: What a LATER phase found wrong with this one, which is why control came back here. Absent on the way down. Shapes differ by sender — a review finding carries `severity`/`claim`/`lens`, a design finding raised by acceptance or implementation carries whatever that phase recorded — so read each entry for what it says rather than expecting one shape.
